asset.description:
Choosing a Canva Template

Once you have reviewed the Multimodal Assignments: Graphic Design library guide, it's time to get started by choosing a Canva template. Browse through templates by searching for "story book" and selecting Canva Templates. You can further refine your search results by clicking "All Filters" and selecting styles, themes, grade levels, and more.

When selecting your template, look for a structure that will fit your story. Don't worry about the pictures, fonts, or color schemes because you can change those. You can create a blank Story Book and build your structure from scratch, but here are some recommended templates. These templates are more text-heavy with only decorative illustrations, because your assignment asks you to use typography to tell your story rather than draw illustrations.

Canva Templates

asset.name: "Exploring Word Origins Story Book"
asset.description: This template is designed for 4th grade and features a bright color palette with lots of text boxes.

asset.name: "What's the Point of View? Story Book"
asset.description: This Story Book template is mostly text but has spots for relevant illustrations.

asset.name: "Relative Clause Guided Tour Story Book"
asset.description: This template mostly uses shapes to provide visual interest with plenty of room for creative typography.

asset.name: "Colorful Lined About Pets Storybook"
asset.description: This template includes different styles of curved text.

Built-in Typography Tools

Once you have chosen your template, you can start editing. Canva includes lots of fonts that you can use to move your story forward, as well as some text effects. These features can all be found in the text edit toolbar, which opens when you select a textbox.

Exploring Fonts

You may want to include multiple fonts to indicate different sounds, characters, or emotions. You can change the font, color, size, or style by using the text edit bar. Canva only allows you to use one font in a text box, so you can use multiple text boxes to combine different fonts like in the example Click, Clack, Moo.

 

 

 

Canva Text Effects

Canva has built-in effects that let you add a shadow or outline to the text, use color effects, place the text on a curve, and more. Click the Effects button in the text edit bar to open the Effects menu. Click on the effect you want to use. Canva will automatically apply the default settings for that effect to your text, but you can customize it in the Effects menu.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Here are some examples of different Effects.

Shadow

The shadow Effect adds a shadow to your text, making a slightly 3D effect.

 

Outline

The outline Effect adds an outline to each letter, providing emphasis and visual interest.

 

Curve

The curve Effect places your text on a circle. You can give the curve a smile effect by using a negative number for the curve, and a frown effect by using a positive number for the curve.

Third-Party Apps

In addition to Canva's built-in tools, Canva offers a number of third-party apps that you can use to manipulate your text. The apps below allow more options for creating different shapes with your text, and are only a few of the many apps available. You can search for apps by clicking the "Apps" button on the left side of the Canva interface, then enter "text" into the search bar.

When using these tools, be very thoughtful about the fonts you use. Creating a shape with  your text may make the text harder to read, so make sure to use fonts that will be clear and legible in the shape.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Recommendations

TypeCraft

Using handle controls, you can bend, warp, and twist the text to create your own shapes filled with your text by using TypeCraft. TypeCraft has a limited number of fonts, so you may not get as many choices as with the built-in features or other apps, but you do get complete control over the shape of your text.

 

Type Warp

Type Warp offers pre-set, simple but customizable shapes that you can use add flair and meaning to your text. Although you have less control over your shapes, it offers all the fonts available with a free Canva account.

Type Curve

This app creates shapes in a different way than the others in this list. Instead of creating a shape out of the letters in your textbox, Type Curve places the letters on a shape. It offers more than 25 shapes ranging from simple squares and triangles to more complicated shapes like spirals, stars, and even a duck. You can select from all the fonts available for a free Canva account, and adjust the spacing between the letters so that all of the text appears on your shape.

Type Extrude

This app creates a 3D effect with your text. You can select your font and color, as well as an outline color. This outline is what creates the 3D effect, and you can choose your own angle and length to make different effects.

Introduction

This guide will help you create your children's book for your class Race and Childhood in American History. You are writing an original historical narrative based on your research about youth activism in Chattanooga, and are expected to use Canva to put the book together. This guide will help you identify and use tools in Canva that will support storytelling through typography.

If you are not familiar with Canva, please refer to our guide on graphic design in Canva linked below. If you need more help with Canva or creating a visual narrative through typography, stop by the Studio on the 3d floor of the Library or schedule a 1-on-1 consultation with a member of the Studio team.

The last section provides instructions for finding current and historical data using library databases (PolicyMap and Social Explorer).

asset.description: This portal contains data collected from the City of Chattanooga as well as the community. The goal of the Chattanooga Open Data Portal is to be the primary location for all open data to be utilized by its citizens.

asset.name: Hamilton County Election Commission Archive
asset.description: Archive of Hamilton County, TN election results from 1990-present.

asset.name: Hamilton County Health Department
asset.description: A variety of health resources, including data, from the Hamilton County Health Department.

asset.name: Tennessee Department of Health Statistics
asset.description: Comprehensive State of Tennessee data and statistics.

asset.name: Tennessee State Data Center
asset.description: The Tennessee State Data Center is a cooperative program of the State of Tennessee, The University of Tennessee and the U.S. Census Bureau. Data Centers in each state assist the Bureau by disseminating Census data, as well as other federal data sets and information.

asset.name: UTC Institutional Dashboards
asset.description: The Institutional and Departmental Dashboards represent a multi-year summary of UTC and its colleges, departments and programs.
Some text about commonalities between the two databases, as well as important differences. Link to Data & Statistics tab?

Maybe some text based instructions?

  • Enter location
    • Select best option from list
  • Browse data categories
    • Top menus expand to reveal more granular data

Maybe some text-based instructions?

  • Explore maps

  • Search for location
    • In the location menu, Center on map layer, and close or collapse menu
  • Change data
    • Select year of interest

  • Create story from data

    • "Tell a story" by making a powerpoint out of your findings

Images

We recommend using these databases to find images for your creative projects instead of using Google Images. By using these image databases, you can generally find higher quality images. You also don't need to worry about copyright issues when you use images from royalty-free sites.

Stock Photos

Stock photos are high-quality, fairly generic photographs that have been licensed for anyone to use. You might have heard of some stock photo companies like Getty Images, which usually require paying either a subscription for the service or a one-time fee for the photo. Below is a list of free stock photo sites. Before using photos from these sites for commercial purposes, double-check the terms of the license.

Best Bets

asset.name: Pexels
asset.description: Pexels offers high quality photos and videos that are tagged and searchable. All the photos and videos on the site are licensed under the Pexels license, so you can use them for free for both commercial and non-commercial projects.

asset.name: Pixabay
asset.description: Pixabay offers royalty-free images, video, audio, and other content under Pixabay's Content License. Check the Content License for specific permissions.

asset.name: Unsplash
asset.description: Unsplash has a large database of photos and illustrations. The Unsplash license allows for free downloads for both commercial and non-commercial purposes.

Other Stock Photo Sites

These stock photo sites may have more targeted collections, or fewer options in general. Some may have their own site licenses, or use Creative Commons licenses. Make sure to check the license for anything you want to use.

asset.name: Biodiversity Heritage Library
asset.description: Download more than 150,000 botanical and animal illustrations for free through Flickr.

asset.name: Flickr: Creative Commons
asset.description:
This search engine lets you find all the photos on Flickr that are licensed under Creative Commons. Creative Commons licenses require attribution in order to be reused, so make sure to cite/attribute where necessary!
Note: Not all Flickr photos are available for reuse, so make sure to check the specifics for every image you find in this search.

asset.name: MorgueFile
asset.description: This is a free photo archive "for creatives, by creatives." The name might sound morbid but it comes from a term used by newspapers to describe inactive job files used for reference.

asset.name: Openverse
asset.description: Openverse aggregates public domain and Creative Commons licensed images and audio from across the internet into a single search tool. Note that the search results are not curated and you must check the license for each image or track you'd like to use.

Fine Art

The art museums below are part of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access Initiative, and provide access to free, unrestricted images of the public-domain art in their collections.

asset.name: Art Institute of Chicago Open Access Collection
asset.description: Over 60,000 public domain images of artworks are available to download and use in your projects.

asset.name: Cleveland Museum of Art
asset.description: You can download more than 40,000 images of artworks for free from the Cleveland Museum of Art.

asset.name: The Met Museum Art Collection
asset.description: Nearly 500,000 images of public-domain artworks are available to download and use for free.

asset.name: National Gallery of Art
asset.description: Over 60,000 images from the National Gallery of Art's collection can be downloaded for free.

asset.name: The Smithsonian Collections
asset.description: There are more than 5 million images from the Smithsonian that can be downloaded for free! This search page lets you search for specific pieces or browse by Smithsonian museum

Illustrations and Vector Graphics

Vector graphics are images made from lines, points, shapes, and curves using software like Adobe Illustrator. They can be scaled to almost any size without losing image quality.

asset.name: Vecteezy
asset.description: This site is one of the largest vector graphics communities in the world. Most files are available for a free account but require attribution.

asset.name: Pixabay Vectors
asset.description: Pixabay offers royalty-free vector images and other content under Pixabay's Content License. Check the Content License for specific permissions.

Other stock photo sites

These sites offer stock photos of specific demographics, or provide photos with Creative Commons licenses.

asset.name: AllGo
asset.description: AllGo is a database of free stock photos focused on including more body types than are typically found in stock photos. Attribution is requested, and AllGo provides the attribution.

asset.name: Disabled and Here Collection
asset.description: Disabled and Here is a community-led effort to provide stock photos and illustrations that celebrate people with disabilities who are often not seen in stock photos. All the images are licensed under a Creative Commons BY 4.0 license, and can be used for any purpose as long as credit is given.

asset.name: The Gender Spectrum Collection
asset.description:
The Gender Spectrum Collection is a stock photo collection focused on offering representation of people beyond the gender binary
This collection aims to help media better represent members of these communities as people not necessarily defined by their gender identities—people with careers, relationships, talents, passions, and home lives.

The photos are licensed under Creative Commons BY-NC-ND 4.0, so they cannot be used commercially and you cannot change the pictures.

asset.name: Images of Empowerment
asset.description: Images of Empowerment is a collection of free images that celebrate women’s lives and work in low- and middle-income countries around the world. The photos are licensed under Creative Commons BY-NC 4.0. They must have proper attribution and cannot be used commercially.

asset.name: The Jopwell Collection Vol 1
asset.description: Free stock images of communities at work. The images from Jopwell can be used freely as long as you include a visible attribution to Jopwell.

asset.name: Picnoi
asset.description: Picnoi is a cooperatively-run stock photo library that looks to expand the kinds of people portrayed in stock photography. You can download images for free and even submit your own pictures to the collection!

asset.name: WOCinTech
asset.description: Women of Color in Tech is a collection featuring women working in technology fields. All the images are licensed under Creative Commons BY, so you must provide attribution but can use the images any way you want. Note that you may need a Flickr account to download the pictures.
Stock Video

asset.name: Pexels Video
asset.description: Pexels offers high quality photos and videos that are tagged and searchable. All the photos and videos on the site are licensed under the Pexels license, so you can use them for free for both commercial and non-commercial projects.

asset.name: Pixabay Videos
asset.description: Pixabay offers royalty-free images, video, audio, and other content under Pixabay's Content License. Check the Content License for specific permissions.

asset.name: Videezy
asset.description: Videezy has stock video footage, Adobe After Effects templates, and more. You can download many of the videos for free for personal and educational use, but check the license if you want to use the footage commercially.

asset.name: Vidsplay
asset.description: Vidsplay is a database of totally free stock video footage, just include an attribution for each video you use.

Audio

There are different kinds of audio that you can download. This section is divided into music resources and sound effects sources.

Music

asset.name: Free Music Archive
asset.description: Free Music Archive is a database of free and high-quality music from a wide range of genres. Music on FMA is licensed under Creative Commons and can be used for free in videos, podcasts, and more. Just make sure you follow the license for any songs you wish to use.

asset.name: Pixabay Music
asset.description: In addition to images and videos, Pixabay offers royalty free music and sound effects that you can download and use in podcasts, videos, and more.

asset.name: YouTube Audio Library
asset.description: YouTube offers a large selection of royalty-free music and sound effects. This link takes you to your YouTube channel dashboard, so you need to be logged into a Google account in order to access the library.
Sound Effects

asset.name: BBC sound effects
asset.description: BBC Sound Effects has more than 33,000 audio clips from around the world. You can download them for free but make sure to check the license information.

asset.name: Freesound
asset.description: Freesound is a collaborative database of sounds that you can download and use for free. The recordings in Freesound are posted with Creative Commons licenses, so check the license for each sound to make sure you can use it in your project.

asset.name: Free Sound Effects
asset.description: This site has thousands of sound effects you can download and use for free, as well as other sounds available for purchase.

asset.name: Pixabay Sound Effects
asset.description: In addition to images and videos, Pixabay offers royalty free music and sound effects that you can download and use in podcasts, videos, and more.

asset.name: Sound Gator
asset.description: Download sound effects for free and use them in videos, podcasts, presentations, and pretty much any other kind of project.
Fonts

asset.name: dafont
asset.description: A collection of mostly free fonts that you can download and install on your computer.
Icons

asset.name: The Noun Project
asset.description: Millions of icons that have been professionally curated and can be downloaded as a PNG or SVG file. Free downloads require attribution.

About this guide

This guide will help you find pictures, video, audio, and other forms of media that you can use for free in just about any project you want. The websites and databases linked here contain material that is in the public domain, licensed under Creative Commons, or is otherwise available through a royalty-free license.

Remember to read the fine print and terms & conditions before using any media that you didn't make yourself!

asset.description: <iframe width=1000 height=500 src="https://utk.co1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_0MqLNXlae6RGKFw"></iframe>

Remixing Graphics with Adobe Express

Adobe Express is a cloud-based graphic design tool that is great for beginners, and it lets you easily create custom graphics for social media and more. Even better, you get access to Adobe Express Premium when you log in with your Mocs ID!

This guide will introduce you to Adobe Express and how to use it to remix existing images to create your own unique graphics. Adobe Express is beginner-friendly with a drag-and-drop interface, so you can feel confident using it even if it's your first graphic design project.

Once you've made your custom design, you can visit the Hatch It! Lab Makerspace to turn your idea into a button or put it on a t-shirt.

asset.name: Adobe Express Studio pathfinder
asset.description: This PDF made by the Studio team provides an introduction to using Adobe Express, including features not included in this guide.

Generative AI in Adobe Express

Adobe Express includes many tools powered by Adobe Firefly, Adobe's AI image generator. This guide will explain some of those tools in more detail, but this is a brief overview of Adobe Express's generative AI features. Adobe Express includes templates and images already created with AI, and has generative AI add-ons that you can add to your workspace. You can also use AI to:

  • generate images using text prompts
  • use text effects to make words that looks like balloons, flowers, and more
  • create document templates
  • remove backgrounds or objects from, or add images to, images

Before using any of the AI features in Adobe Express, check your assignment or syllabus to make sure that these features fall under your professor's acceptable use of AI. Remember that each of your professors may have a different AI policy and what is acceptable in one class may not be allowed in another class.

Planning Your Design

Before you start working in Adobe Express, start by thinking about what you want to make. Your final product may help inform some of your design choices. Taking some time to plan out your project also allows you to organize your ideas and the information you want to convey. Here are some questions to think about before you get started:

  • What do you want your end product to be?
    This may help you determine the size and shape of your design. For example, if you want to make buttons then you'll need to know what size the button maker is. If you're making a 3" button, then you will want to make sure that your design fits inside a 3" circle.
  • What do you plan to do with your design?
    Let's say you are designing something that you plan to sell. As you're putting your design together, make sure that you are only choosing elements that can be used commercially. 
  • What is the purpose of your design?
    Adobe Express can be used to make anything from presentations to logos to stickers. Think about what information you're trying to convey through your project and how you can best communicate it to your audience. If you're making a social media post, how would the design be different if you were making it for your public Instagram account, your finsta, or the account for your small business?

Logging in to Adobe Express

The first step to using Adobe Express is to log in. You don't need to create an account, because you already have an Adobe Express account as a student at UTC. In order to use your free Adobe account, you do need to follow these steps to log in.

  1. Go to Adobe Express (linked below), then click Sign In.
  2. Enter @tennessee.edu as the email address, then click Continue. You will go to the UT System Central Authentication Service.
  3. On the CAS page, login with your UTC ID and password. You may need to log in using DUO mobile.

You may be redirected to the general Adobe launch screen. If you are, click the Express link at the top of the page.

Logging in to Adobe Express

The first step to using Adobe Express is to log in. In order to use all the features of Adobe Express, it's best to have a student account. You can get a free 6 month trial for a student account:

  1. Go to Adobe Express (link below).
  2. Create an account using a non-UTC email address.
  3. Make a new account as a higher ed student.

You should not be asked for any payment information when making a free account. If you are, go back and make sure that you're signing up for a free account. After 6 months you can switch your account to a standard free account, which has fewer features but still works great.

Create a project

Once you log in to Adobe Express, you will go to the home screen. This is where you can decide what kind of project you're working on. There are templates for Instagram stories and posts, flyers, presentations, logos, and more. You can browse all the templates by clicking the "Templates" icon on the left side of the screen. From here, you can use the filters to narrow down your template choices. Once you've chosen a template, you can start customizing it for your design. Or, if none of the templates work for you, you can also create a blank project.

Explore the interface

Before you start working in Adobe Express for the first time, take a few minutes to get to know the interface. The web-based workspace is divided into 3 main sections:

  1. The Stuff Panel is on the left-hand side of the screen, and this is where you can find anything you'd like to add to your design. You'll notice that there are icons for templates, media, text, and more. When you click the icons in the Stuff Panel, the panel will expand so you can search and browse for things to add to your design:
    • Templates: start a new design with a template
    • Media: find stock photos, videos, and audio from Adobe Stock (included with your UTC Adobe account)
    • Text: add plain text boxes or stylized text templates
    • Elements: find shapes and icons, as well as illustrations and other graphics (search under Design Assets)
    • Charts and grids: add tables, charts, and graphs
    • Generative AI: create images, text effects, and custom templates using Adobe's Gen AI tool Firefly
  2. The File menu is at the top of the window. This section also has tools to let you resize and rename your design, find preset color themes, and share your design.
  3. The Canvas is the main part of the window and where you will work on your design.

Once you're familiar with the interface, you can start designing. For this guide, we're going to look at adding and remixing photos.

Add Images

Adding Images from Adobe Express

You can find photos (as well as videos and audio) by clicking the Media button. Search or browse media from Adobe Stock by clicking Photos, Videos, or Audio at the top of the stuff panel. Click the picture you want to use so you can add it to your canvas.

Upload Your Own Picture

If you can't find the picture you want to use in Adobe Express, or if you want to use one of your own pictures, you easily can upload your own. Click the Upload button and find the picture on your device, and it will automatically be added to your canvas.

Editing Pictures

Whether you add your own photo or use one that you found in Adobe Express, you can edit them with the same tools.

With the picture selected, you can edit it and apply effects with the Stuff panel. Play around with some of the edit options. You can always use the undo button (the backwards arrow icon, CTRL+Z, or CMD+Z on a Mac) if you don't like it. The Edit section has options like removing the background or removing an object with just one click. Click Adjust to change the brightness, color saturation, and more. Crop your photo to a different size or shape by double-clicking on the picture.

Removing the background

You can make your own photo cutouts and remove the background of an image with one click! With the image selected, just click the Remove Background button in the Stuff panel.

Removing an object from a picture

You can also remove an unwanted object from a picture, whether it's a person walking through your shot or a blemish in your headshot. With the image selected, click the Remove Object button in the Stuff panel. You'll be able to select everything you want to remove from the picture by drawing over it with your mouse. When you have the entire thing painted over with the remover brush, click the Remove button. Adobe Express uses AI to remove the object and fill in the hole based on what's in the rest of your image. It gives you 3 options to choose from, and if you don't like any of them you can generate more. When you have a version you like, click the Keep button.

Add text

Click the Text button in the Stuff panel to start adding text to your design. You can add a plain text box using the "Add your text" button at the top of the panel, but you can also choose from a lots of text templates made by Adobe's designers. The templates are separated by category, including:

  • Dates
  • Buttons
  • Stickers
  • Paragraphs
  • Phrases

All the templates are completely customizable, and you can use them for anything. Don't limit yourself by only using the text templates based on their category. Adobe Express also has a tool that uses generative AI to make text effects. You can use this to make text that looks like balloons, disco balls, plants, and more. You have so many options to get creative!

Once you've added a text box, double-click it to change your text. You'll notice that the Stuff panel switches to a text editor panel. This is where you can change the font, color, and size of your text. There are also formatting tools that work just like the tools in Microsoft Word or Google Docs.

There are also other tools you won't usually find in a text documents, like making shapes with your text. Click the Text Layouts button to turn your text into a complete or partial circle. Click the Effects menu to add decorative elements to your text. You can add shadows, borders, and more to your text. These are great tools to explore when making logos!

You can also find filters, add shadows, and apply color filters under Effects. You can even use multiple layers to make your images pop. This lets you really start making your design unique, which is particularly important if you plan on selling your design.

Add Elements

Adobe Express offers many shapes, icons, and other graphics that you can use to customize your design. Click the Elements icon to see your options in the Stuff panel. Once the Elements menu is open, you can search or browse for:

  • Backgrounds: photos, illustrations, and other graphics that are especially good to use as the background of a design. You can also use a plain color as a background, or upload your own image and click "Set background" in the image edit menu.
  • Shapes: simple shapes, lines, arrows, and speech bubbles. You can also draw your own shapes and choose your own colors for all shapes.
  • Icons: icons and line drawings of animals, plants, people, and more. Like shapes, you can choose the color of any icon you use.
  • Design assets: essentially anything that doesn't fit in one of the other categories can be found under design assets. You can find illustrations,  photo cutouts, pre-made collages, textures, and more. Objects found in design assets work like images, and in general you can't change their colors.
  • Stickers: stickers are animated graphics that you can add to images, videos, and other projects in Adobe Express. If you add stickers, make sure that you download your project as either a .MP4 video or a .GIF image so that the animation works.

Once you have found an element you want in your design, just click and drag to add it to your canvas. Then you can treat it like any other part of your design, moving it and resizing it however you want.

Layers

Adobe Express, like other Adobe tools, uses layers, and explains layers as "transparent folders for managing content." This can be very helpful when organizing your design.

In Adobe Express each object you add to your design (pictures, text, etc.) is its own layer, and you can find them all in the "layers stack" on the right side of your canvas. Click on the layers icon to see all the layers in your project. The layers are in the order of how you added each item, but you can click and drag the layers to reorder them. Whatever is on the top of the layer stack will show up on top of the other layers in your canvas.

You can group objects together so that they work like one object. If you have multiple things in your project that you want to keep together, hold down the shift key on your keyboard and select all the objects you want to stay together. In the toolbar that pops up on the canvas, click "group." This turns the group of objects into one layer, and they'll stay together whenever you move them around.

Share Your Design

Adobe Express is cloud-based, so it auto-saves your project as you make changes just like Google Docs or Microsoft Word 365. When you're done designing your project, you'll need to either download it or otherwise share it.

If you are working on a project for a class, you will probably need to download it. Click the Download button at the top of the workspace to save a copy to your phone or computer. Adobe Express will let you choose your file type, but it will also make a recommendation based on what's in your design.

Adobe Express also lets you connect to your social media accounts so you can share an image or video directly to Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, and more. You can find all the sharing options by clicking the Share button.

Convert Your Design to SVG

If you want to turn your design into a physical object at the Hatch It! Lab, you may need to turn it into an SVG file first. You can convert any image into an SVG using Adobe Express.

Before you start, make sure that you have the image downloaded to your device. Open the Adobe Express landing page and click the create button. Instead of creating a new project, open the "Quick actions" menu, then click "Convert to SVG." Upload your image and it will automatically be converted to an SVG. Download the SVG file and you will be able to use it to create stickers and objects using Hatch It! Lab equipment like the laser cutter and Cricut. For more information about SVGs, check out the SVG Vector Files for Laser and Vinyl Cutters library guide linked below.

Other Helpful Links

Here are some links that you may find helpful while working on your podcast or any other multimodal assignment.

The UTC Library creates short, easy to follow guides we call "Pathfinders." They are useful for getting started with a new software (like Photoshop), learning a specific skill (Green Screen Keying), or a new setup (Three-Point Lighting). All guides are fully accessible and under a CC-BY-NC license.

The Studio supports five different video editors:

ClipChamp: This is a web-based Microsoft application that lives in 0365. (Free and great for group projects.)

iMovie: This is a Mac-only application that comes free when you buy an Apple device. 

Camtasia:

Adobe Illustrator

Illustrator is Adobe's vector drawing program. You can import existing images or Photoshop files to turn them from rasters into vectors or you can draw your own design directly in the program. It is particularly good for tracing images. 

Starting Your Project

To get started open Illustrator and create a new document. Enter the document name and dimensions in the upper right-hand corner (Next to the dimensions you can change the unit of measurements from Points to any unit of measurement you would like such as Pixels or Inches.  It’s useful to make the dimensions match the dimensions of the physical material that you’ll be cutting/engraving.)

Note: If you are working in the UTC Library Studio and need help signing in, follow these steps.

Existing Images (logo, cat photo, etc.):

First, we need to bring your image into Illustrator or "import" it. Go to File > Place and select the image you would like to import.

Once the image is selected you can place the object onto your document by clicking on the artboard or you can scale the object and place it by clicking and dragging a box to your preferred size. 

If you placed a piece of artwork that is a raster file, we will need to convert it to a vector.  Select the image and go to Object > Image Trace > Make Simpler images usually get better results.

Depending on the quality, colors, or type of image you are working with you might need to change the Image Trace Preset in the Properties window. 

Once you like how your image looks, go to Object > Image Trace > Expand to add paths and anchor points.

After expanding, a grey box will pop up. Click the "Ungroup" button. You can also go to Object > Ungroup or right-click > Ungroup.

 

Next decide if you need to delete the fill color (in this example, it is white). Engravings usually keep the infill, cuts and scores often don't. To delete the infill color, select the area you want to clear and go to select > same > fill color and hit delete. NOTE: This can make it appear that your object has been deleted if it doesn't already have a stroke (outline) set. 

 

Now adjust your stroke. Keep your object selected, and double click on the "Stroke" box below 'Fill' in the Appearance section of the Properties window. Select black. Then adjust the size of the stroke to at least .025 PT. (Laser cutters can't cut any smaller than that.)

Creating a Design from Scratch:

See the Illustrator Guide for information on various tools that can be used for drawing. Photoshop is a great option. The guide is below. Keep in mind the instructions above regarding simplicity, strokes, and fill since they apply to anything you would like do on the machines. 

Exporting for use:

Once you're done you need to save your design as an usable file. Go to File > Save As, and then select your file type.

For cutting or scoring, save your design as an SVG.

For engraving, save your design as a .JPEG or .PNG.

It's always a good idea to save your Illustrator file in case you want to tweak things later.

Be aware of the size of your object.
Check to ensure the design is to scale. You can add a rulers to your workspace by going to View > Rulers > Show Rulers.

Keep things connected.
You may need bridges to help the machine cut cleanly without pieces falling off and getting lost. You can clean things up later with an exacto knife.

Convert your text into shapes or “outlines.”
The machines think of them as weird shapes, so this ensures a cleaner result.

Remove all intersecting lines
If you have overlapping artwork, go in and remove any extra lines since the machines will still try to cut them. Combining objects can also help make things simpler and avoid unpleasant surprises.

Eliminate open shapes
Shapes that are open and unfinished will not work with a laser cutter. Ensure all paths are connected.

Reduce the complexity of your design where possible
In general, the more complex your design the greater possibility for failure or breakage. Start simple and iterate as you learn more about how the machines function.

This research guide is an invitation to engage with resources that document Indigenous history, knowledge, and experiences of place in Chattanooga and the Southeast region.

The Southeastern Woodlands have been inhabited since time immemorial and are the ancestral home of many Indigenous nations, in particular the S’atsoyaha (Yuchi), Mvskoke (Creek), and the ᏣᎳᎫᏪᏘᏱ Tsalaguwetiyi (Cherokee), whose relationship to these lands, waters, and skies continues to this day. After forcible relocation by the federal government in the 1830s with the Indian Removal Act, many in these nations moved west into Oklahoma.

In Chattanooga, the Trail of Tears endures as the primary framework for understanding the relationship between Chattanooga and Indigenous peoples. Constant reminders of removal and dispossession, Trail of Tears signs dot the city, reinforcing the myth that Native presence “ended” in 1838 and is irrelevant to later history and the contemporary moment. Yet Native presence endures and a goal of this guide is to foreground under-recognized narratives of survivance, continued engagement with place, and efforts to build a future grounded in care for these lands.

As you engage with this research guide, we invite you all to consider your own relationship to these lands and the communities who have long stewarded them.

asset.name: Native Land Digital
asset.description: Native Land Digital (NLD) is an Indigenous-led non-profit organization that provides a digital map of Indigenous territories, languages, and treaties globally. Use their tools as a starting point for engagement with Indigenous histories and communities.

This collection of resources emerges from a 2025-2026 Walker Center for Teaching and Learning Faculty Fellows Working Group aiming to deepen UTC’s ties to place by prioritizing Indigenous perspectives on the city and wider region. UTC plays a critical role as a repository of interdisciplinary knowledge of the history of the place we live and work. Our working group convened in response to our shared responsibility to this place, the UTC student body, and the community at large.

This guide was created by Natalie Blanton, Molly Copeland, Chelsea Couch, Amber Hickey, Emma McDonell, Brooke Persons, Bart Pushaw, and Kylie Williamson, none of whom claim authority to speak from lived experience or on behalf of Indigenous communities. These resources have been compiled with an emphasis on centering the perspectives of those who can. We welcome feedback on this living document.

Please direct feedback and questions to Molly Copeland, Manuscripts Archivist in Special Collections.

Chattanooga is the ancestral home to Indigenous nations that are present and thriving today. Those Indigenous nations are documented through oral traditions, historic documents, tribal knowledge, and the archaeological past. Some of the Native nations who call Chattanooga home are Federally Recognized Tribes, and there are many tribal communities that lack formal federal recognition. Additionally, there are a number of national and local organizations that share information about tribal history of the region.

asset.description: There are no state or federally recognized tribes in Tennessee; however, there are several organizations created by and for Native Americans in the state that provide services and host educational and cultural programming.

box.name: Visting and Researching Historic and Commemorative Sites

asset.description:
The physical and cultural landscape that we inhabit reflects the successes, challenges, survival, and resistance of Indigenous peoples before, during, and after the arrival of settlers. These stories are embedded in the sites, museums, and commemorative spaces that dot the landscape and surround our everyday lives in the city and broader region. Many sites are accessible to the public, some of which are highlighted below.

Use the following resources to plan visits to these local sites or as the starting point for further research.

If you have any questions or need help with research, stop by the Research Services Desk on the second floor of the Library, or visit the Library's Help page for other ways to seek research assistance.

• Brainerd Mission
  • Moccasin Bend
  • Monumental Earthworks
  • Red Clay State Historic Park

asset.description: Run by the Chattanooga Audubon Society, Audubon Acres is a historic site and nature preserve near the historic Little Owl Village, a historic Cherokee village, and is recognized as a part of the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail. This museum features educational outreach programs and nature trails, offering different avenues for learning about Indigenous lifeways.

asset.name: Audubon Acres, Chattanooga Audubon Society
asset.description: Chattanooga Audubon Society's official website for Audubon Acres with information for visitors, site history, and information about educational programming, including the Little Owl Lecture Series.

The Brainerd Mission Cemetery is the only intact remnant of the Brainerd Mission. Active from 1817 to 1838, this large settlement was a prominent site in the Christianization of the Cherokee people. In the following century, the Brainerd Mission Cemetery has often been central to historical preservation interests in the city and was successfully registered on the National Register of Historic Sites. After intense commercial development along Brainerd Road since the 1950s, the cemetery is now sandwiched between the Brainerd Village Shopping Center and the Eastgate Town Center. The cemetery is enclosed by a fence with a locked gate, but people wishing to visit the cemetery can request an appointment by calling (423) 987-0405, leaving a message including your name, phone number, and reason for your request. Messages containing these details will be returned within 48 hours.

asset.name: West, Carroll Van and Sarah Jackson Martin, "Brainerd Mission Cemetery: property survey and history" (2006). Center for Historic Preservation, Middle Tennessee State University.
asset.description: A property survey and history of the Brainerd Mission Cemetery prepared in 2006 for the Southern Places Project at Middle Tennessee State University's Center for Historic Preservation.

asset.name: “Brainerd Mission Cemetery, Chattanooga,” Trail Of Tears National Historic Trail, National Park Service.
asset.description: Site information provided by the National Park Service.

asset.name: Penelope Johnson Allen Brainerd Mission correspondence and photographs digital collection, Chattanooga Public Library and the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga Special Collections
asset.description: The Penelope Johnson Allen Brainerd Mission correspondence and photographs digital collection features orignal correspondence and receipts created by the United States Department of War, Indian Agent Return J. Meigs, and Brainerd Mission superintendents and founders Gideon Blackburn, Cyrus Kingsbury, and Ard Hoyt. The collection also includes photographs of portraits of the Brainerd missionaries, Daughters of the American Revolution dedication events at Brainerd Mission Cemetery, and copies of etchings of Brainerd Mission.

asset.name: Nancy Reece Cherokee sampler, 1832. 2016.260, Tennessee State Museum.
asset.description: This sampler at the Tennessee State Museum was created at Brainerd Mission in 1823 by Nancy Reece. The sampler is the earliest known example of a sampler made by a young Cherokee woman. Reece married Joseph Starr in 1836 and had three children. Her first child was born on the Trail of Tears in 1837. After the forced removal of the Cherokee people from the Southeast, Nancy Reece died in present-day Oklahoma in 1875.

asset.name: Moccasin Bend National Archeological District Google Map

asset.description: The Moccasin Bend Archaeological District is protected as part of the National Park Service’s Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park. The 956-acre park protects numerous sites, features, and earthworks that represent more than 12,000 years of continuous human occupation. Beginning with the initial settlement of the region by 10,000 BC, Moccasin Bend later saw the rise of tribal nations as well as later interaction with early Spaniards in the 1500s, the intrusion of European settlers, the introduction of enslavement through plantation economies, the fight for Emancipation through the Underground Railroad, and the Battle for Chattanooga during the Civil War. Communities here flourished, fought, and struggled to survive cataclysmic cultural change both predating and enduring European contact. As the only National Historic Landmark in Hamilton County, Moccasin Bend mirrors the broad spectrum of human history in East Tennessee.

asset.name: Moccasin Bend National Archeological District
asset.description: The National Park Service's history timeline of Moccasin Bend.

asset.name: 10,000 Years of History: A Field Trip on the American Indians of North Georgia and East Tennessee
asset.description: The National Park Service offers ranger-led school field trips to Moccasin Bend National Archeological District.

asset.name: National Park Partners
asset.description: National Park Partners is a Chattanooga-base nonprofit dedicated to championing the conservation of the natural, historic, and cultural resources of Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park, including Moccasin Bend National Archeological District. The organization combined two advocacy groups, Friends of the Park (established 1986) and Friends of Moccasin Bend. Friend of Moccasin Bend was formed in 1995 to advocate for the inclusion of 750 acres of historically and culturally significant land on Moccasin Bend into National Park Service protection.

asset.name: Moccasin Bend Lecture Series
asset.description: Presented by National Park Partners, the Moccasin Bend Lecture Series offers three unique lectures each fall with speakers and topics related to National Parks and conservation; Indigenous culture and history; and Chattanooga’s place in the U.S. Civil War. Recordings of previous lectures are available on the organization's YouTube Channel.

Indigenous peoples began building monumental earthworks or mounds beginning around 350 CE. As living monuments created through communal rituals, mounds created sacred spaces, honored ancestors, and built community.

Chickamauga Mound

The only mound in the area that is easily accessible and intact today, Chickamauga mound and neighboring village were constructed between 350-900 CE and maintained prior to European settlement. Many peoples contributed to the development of the site, including the Yuchi, Creek, and Cherokee peoples, and more. The Chickamauga Mound, also known as the Roxbury Mound, was partially preserved thanks to community advocacy and tribal consultation, although the surrounding village was heavily impacted by industrial development.

asset.name: Campbell, Virginia, "The Untold Story of Native American Activism in Chattanooga," Rising Rock, February 2, 2022.

asset.description:
Citico Mound

Similar to the Chickamauga Mound, the Citico Mound was built and maintained since 350 CE. A central focal point of ceremony and public life for the surrounding village, the Citico Mound experienced a very different trajectory than the nearby Chickamauga Mound. Following the forced removal of tribal nations through the Trail of Tears, the depopulated mound site was desecrated when the Union Army built a munitions depot on top of the mound during the Civil War (1861-1865), in addition to planting limited crops. The mound was subsequently destroyed in the early 1910s when the J. Wells Brick Company mined the mound for clay minerals. The remainder of the Citico site and mound was later impacted by the construction of Amnicola Highway and nearby developments. While pockets of the surrounding village remain preserved, the memory of the Citico Mound marks a substantial desecration of heritage and history.

asset.name: Honerkamp, Nicholas, “Whatever Happened to Citico Mound,” Chattanooga Times Free Press, March 1, 2015.

asset.description:
Ross's Landing

Today, Ross's Landing in downtown Chattanooga is a riverfront park, a tourist destination, home to many community events and concerts, and the doorstep to the Tennessee Aquarium. We invite you to sit with this paradox, and see this place not as a neutral "historic landmark," but as a scar and a testament: the principal point of departure for the Trail of Tears (ᏅᎾ ᏓᎤᎳ ᎢᏍᏗ, Nunna daul Isunyi — "The Trail Where They Cried"). 


In the 1810s, Principal Chief John Ross (ᎫᏫᏍᎫᏫ, Guwisguwi) of the Cherokee Nation established a ferry landing and trading post on this section of the southern bank of the Tennessee River. In June 1838, despite the Cherokee Nation having won its right to remain before the U.S. Supreme Court (Worcester v. Georgia), over 1,500 Cherokee people were gathered here and forced onto boats and barges heading west. Over 800 miles and several months, hundreds died from exposure, starvation, and illness before ever reaching "Indian Territory" (present-day Oklahoma). Ross, who fought the Removal Act for a decade, —and then was forced to lead his own people into exile. Between 1838 and 1839, Ross’s Landing became the departure point for the organized detachments and immediately adjacent areas in downtown Chattanooga also served as holding camps where Indigenous people were forcibly relocated and guarded prior to the westward journey. While the original landing is submerged as a result of the damming of the Tennessee River and the creation of the Chickamauga Reservoir in the late 1930s, Ross’s Landing remains a somber site of remembrance.

box.name: UTC Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation (NAGPRA) Policy

asset.name: University of Tennessee at Chattanooga Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Ace Policy
asset.description: The University's NAGPRA Policy, passed in November 2023.

As an institution receiving federal funding and housing archaeological collections, UTC is obligated to comply with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990 (NAGPRA) and its implementing regulations. This federal legislation requires institutions to consult with federally recognized tribes and to repatriate Ancestral Human Remains, Funerary Objects, Sacred Objects, and Objects of Cultural Patrimony to lineal descendants. Repatriation, transferring legal custody of a collection to another party, is an important step that returns sensitive collections under UTC’s care to federally recognized descendant tribes.

UTC remains committed to transparent and respectful consultation as UTC completes its NAGPRA inventory, which involves a review of all archaeological collections cared for by UTC. To that end, UTC established a NAGPRA committee and approved a university-wide NAGPRA Policy governing the use of NAGPRA collections in teaching and research in November 2023. UTC’s NAGPRA committee aspires to work in the spirit of NAGPRA to manage collections and conduct research in ways that meet our obligation to tribal partners, honoring communities past and present.

As you explore this guide, ask yourself: 

  • How do these resources help you reflect on your own relationship to place?
  • What was your early education about Indigenous Communities in your area? How was that framed?
  • Whose histories are commemorated in Chattanooga? Whose are  missing? Who or what do the silences serve?
  • How does the history of this place or the your own community make you feel?
  • Whose history is carved into the benches, plaques, and walking paths of Ross's Landing or the Trail of Tears commemoration sites? 
  • How is Chattanooga framed and who is missing from the tourist brochures? And what would it mean to treat this site as a cemetery—and a classroom—rather than a backdrop for recreation?
  • How might we also sense and support ongoing Indigenous survivance in our region?

UTC Special Collections provides free and open access to cultural heritage resources that document Chattanooga, Tennessee, and the South, including the history of the university. Below is an non-exhaustive list of materials related to Chattanooga's Indigenous history. Learn more about accessing materials in Special Collection by visiting the Special Collections website or Ask an Archivist.

asset.name: Penelope Johnson Allen papers
asset.description: This collection contains research notes, correspondence, clippings, histories, photographs, receipts, deeds, and research notes on the topics of Brainerd Mission and the Cherokee that were created or collected by Penelope Johnson Allen primarily from 1933 to 1976. The collection also documents the historian's work with the Daughters of the American Revolution to preserve the cemetery at Brainerd Mission in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

asset.name: Anne Bachman Hyde papers
asset.description: This collection includes material relating to the Cherokee Indians and their removal; the Brainerd Mission; the Civil War; the South; the United Daughters of the Confederacy; historical documents, publications and journals, and literature and art.

asset.name: Robert Sparks Walker papers
asset.description: This collection includes correspondence, financial records, scrapbooks, and other personal papers as well as manuscripts and drafts of books, articles, and poetry authored by Robert Sparks Walker, a Chattanooga naturalist, writer, poet, and local historian dating from 1896 to 1962. Highlights of this collection include the manuscript and dummies for Walker's Pulitzer Prize nominated book, Torchlights to the Cherokees: The Brainerd Mission.

asset.name: State of Georgia Cherokee Land Lottery land grant
asset.description: This collection consists of a single land grant issued by the state of Georgia to Richard Banks in 1846.

asset.name: Zach Wamp papers
asset.description: This collection includes the Zach Wamp's congressional and political papers ranging from 1992 to 2010. Wamp was the U.S. representative for Tennessee's 3rd congressional district from 1995 to 2011, and was instrumental in the effort to preserve Moccasin Bend with the creation of the Moccasin Bend National Archaeological District as part of the Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park.

asset.name: Chattanooga oral histories: Gayle Ross Interview
asset.description: This oral history with Gayle Ross, a member of Cherokee Nation, is part of the Chattanooga oral histories collection. This collection contains forty-seven video oral histories with a diverse group of citizens regarding the history of Chattanooga, Tennessee recorded in 2011. The interviews were conducted by TruFILMS as part of the exhibit development work completed by Ralph Appelbaum Associates on behalf of the Chattanooga History Center.

asset.name: Chattanooga oral histories: John Ross interview
asset.description: This oral history with John Ross, a member of Cherokee Nation, is part of the Chattanooga oral histories collection. This collection contains forty-seven video oral histories with a diverse group of citizens regarding the history of Chattanooga, Tennessee recorded in 2011. The interviews were conducted by TruFILMS as part of the exhibit development work completed by Ralph Appelbaum Associates on behalf of the Chattanooga History Center.

This collection contains forty-seven video oral histories with a diverse group of citizens regarding the history of Chattanooga, Tennessee recorded in 2011. The interviews were conducted by TruFILMS as part of the exhibit development work completed by Ralph Appelbaum Associates on behalf of the Chattanooga History Center.

UTC Scholar provides access to the Jeffrey L. Brown Institute of Archaeology Reports, a digital collection containubg reports of archaeological and documentary research in the greater Chattanooga area and the Southeastern United States.

Materials in the Jeffrey L. Brown Institute of Archaeology Reports digital collection are currently under review for compliance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act.

While under review, materials are available for access upon request. Please review the UTC NAGPRA Policy and send inquiries to the NAGPRA Committee.

If you have questions about this series, please contact Brooke Persons, Director, Jeffrey L. Brown Institute of Archaeology.

Finding Primary Sources

Primary sources related to Indigenous history in and around Chattanooga can be found across numerous repositories and online. The following internet resources can help you find relevant primary sources at other institutions.

asset.name: Digital Public Library of America
asset.description: This portal makes it easy to search the digital collections of thousands of United States libraries, archives, and museums, all in one website.

asset.name: National Archives and Records Administration
asset.description: The National Archives preserves and makes available documents created by federal agencies in the course of their daily business. Researchers can find information relating to American Indians and Alaska Natives from as early as 1774 through the mid-1990s at National Archives locations throughout the country.

asset.name: ArchiveGrid
asset.description: ArchiveGrid includes over 7 million records from over 1,400 archival institutions describing archival materials, bringing together information about historical documents, personal papers, family histories, and more.

For a more comprehensive list of resources for databases, as well as tips for finding primary sources beyond the UTC Library, see our Primary Sources Topic Guide.

Featured Primary Sources

Presented here are a few featured archival collections and other primary sources related to Indigenous history in Chattanooga.

asset.name: Z. Cartter Patten and Albert S. Lenoir papers
asset.description: This collection at the Chattanooga Public Library consists of papers and records created by Z. Cartter Patten and his grandfather-in-law, Albert S. Lenoir. Records of Albert S. Lenoir include ration books he created as a Federal issuing agent during Cherokee removal. The handwritten ration books record the names of Cherokee and Creek individuals held at the camps from 1836-1838, along with the volume of various rations they were allotted each week.

asset.name: Cherokee Claims and Related Records digital collection
asset.description: This collection at the Tennessee State Library and Archives contains loose spoliation claims from 1838 and 1842. The loose claims are part of the Penelope Johnson Allen Cherokee Collection. The Penelope Johnson Allen Cherokee Collection spans the years 1775-1878 and contains materials relating to the Cherokees and to John Ross (1790-1866), Principal Chief of the Cherokees, 1828-1866. The collection was purchased from Mrs. Penelope Johnson Allen of Chattanooga, Tennessee, who previously obtained the portion belonging to John Ross from his grandson, Robert Bruce Ross (1845-1930).

asset.description: Use the following databases available at UTC to find academic journal articles and resources in the field of Native American and Indigenous studies and history.

asset.name: Academic OneFile (Gale)
asset.description: Scholarly, peer-reviewed journals, popular news and magazines, and other resources spanning a broad range of disciplines.

asset.name: America History & Life
asset.description: History, culture, area studies, and current affairs literature of the United States and Canada, from prehistory to the present.

asset.name: Anthropological Literature
asset.description: Cultural, linguistic, social and applied anthropology, archaeology, folklore, and more.

asset.name: eHRAF Archaeology
asset.description: eHRAF Archaeology focuses on in-depth descriptive documents of archaeological traditions from around the world.

asset.name: eHRAF World Cultures
asset.description: Contains information on present and past aspects of cultural and social life for a worldwide sample of societies.

asset.name: North American Indian Drama
asset.description: Contains plays by members of the North American Indigenous communities. Includes detailed information on productions, companies, and theaters.
The following are a selection of journals focused on Native American and Indigenous studies and the history of the Southeast.

asset.name: Amercian Indian Quarterly
asset.description: American Indian Quarterly has earned its reputation as one of the dominant journals in American Indian studies by presenting the best and most thought-provoking scholarship in the field. It is a forum for diverse voices and perspectives spanning a variety of academic disciplines. The common thread is the journal’s commitment to publishing work that contributes to the development of American Indian studies as a field and to the sovereignty and continuance of American Indian nations and cultures. In addition to peer-reviewed articles, AIQ features reviews of books, films, and exhibits.

asset.name: American Indian Law Review
asset.description: The American Indian Law Review serves as a nationwide scholarly forum for the presentation and analysis of developments in the law concerning Indigenous people and Indian affairs. Adhering to the traditional law review format, the American Indian Law Review offers in depth articles written by legal scholars, attorneys and other expert observers. In addition, law students write on a wide variety of issues in the rapidly expanding field of Indian law.

asset.name: Cultural Survival Quarterly
asset.description: Cultural Survival Quarterly is the society newsletter for Cultural Survival, an Indigenous-led NGO and U.S. registered non-profit that advocates for Indigenous Peoples' rights and supports Indigenous communities’ self-determination, cultures, and political resilience. This magazine publishes thought-provoking essays, book reviews, and photographs with the intent of expanding public understanding about Indigenous rights and cultures, with writers from Indigenous communities or working closely with Indigenous groups.

asset.name: Ethnohistory
asset.description: Ethnohistory emphasizes the joint use of documentary materials and ethnographic or archaeological data, as well as the combination of historical and anthropological approaches, in the study of social and cultural processes and history. The journal has established a strong reputation for its studies of the history of native peoples in the Americas and in recent years has expanded its focus to cultures and societies throughout the world.

asset.name: Georgia Historical Quarterly
asset.description: The Georgia Historical Quarterly is one of the premier state historical journals in the United States, published quarterly by the Georgia Historical Society. The Quarterly publishes the finest scholarly articles on Georgia history and book reviews dealing with all aspects of southern and Georgia history.

asset.name: NAIS: Journal of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Association
asset.description: NAIS publishes the best interdisciplinary scholarship in international Native American and Indigenous Studies. The journal provides an intellectually rigorous and ethically engaged forum for smart, provocative, and exciting scholarship while drawing on the extraordinary professional expertise of our ever-expanding membership in a process of double-anonymous peer review. NAIS provides a forum to place different kinds of research, intellectual traditions, and knowledge practices in conversation.

asset.name: Native South
asset.description: Native South challenges scholars of southern history to expand their conception of the field to include more than the black and white post-colonial south that colors much of the historical literature of the region. The journal focuses on the investigation of Southeastern Indian history with the goals of encouraging further study and exposing the influences of Indian people on the wider South. It does not limit itself to the study of the geographic area that was once encompassed by the Confederacy, but expands its view to the areas occupied by the pre-contact- and the post-contact descendants of the original inhabitants of the South, wherever they may be.

asset.name: Southern Cultures
asset.description: Published quarterly by UNC's Center for the Study of the American South, Southern Cultures assembles a rich forum of animated, voices discussing all aspects of southern life. Compiling the best of academic and general interest writing, each issue features insightful articles, entertaining columns, and captivating photographs--all bound in an award-winning design. Regular features survey southern foods, personal reminiscences, and contemporary trends.

asset.name: Southern Spaces
asset.description: Southern Spaces is a peer-reviewed, multimedia, open access journal published by the Emory Center for Digital Scholarship. Southern Spaces publishes work in a variety of humanities and social science disciplines that represents and analyzes many souths and southern regions, offers critical scrutiny of any monolithic "South," interrogates historical geographies over time, and maps expressive cultural forms associated with place.

asset.name: Tennessee Historical Quarterly
asset.description: Established in 1942, the Tennessee Historical Quarterly (THQ) appears four times a year. The illustrated articles cover all aspects of Tennessee history, from first European contact to the late 20th century, and all regions of the state, while books reviews cover the latest publications on Tennessee history and related topics. The journal also often includes edited primary documents.

asset.name: Wicazo Sa Review
asset.description: Wicazo Sa Review provides inquiries into the Indian past and its relationship to the vital present. Its aim is to become an interdisciplinary instrument to assist indigenous peoples of the Americas in taking possession of their own intellectual and creative pursuits. Each issue contains articles, essays, interviews, reviews, literary criticism, and scholarly research pertinent to Native American Studies and related fields.

asset.description:
This research guide was put together by UTC Librarians and has links to a variety of resources that you have access to. Use this guide to find:

  • Recommended databases and subscriptions
  • Quick Search box for finding books, articles, movies and more
  • Links to more help

Empirical research is based on observed and measured phenomena and derives knowledge from actual experience rather than from theory or belief. 

How do you know if a study is empirical? Read the subheadings within the article, book, or report and look for a description of the research "methodology." Ask yourself: Could I recreate this study and test these results?

Key characteristics to look for:

  • Specific research questions to be answered
  • Definition of the population, behavior, or phenomena being studied
  • Description of the process used to study this population or phenomena, including selection criteria, controls, and testing instruments (such as surveys)

Another hint: some scholarly journals use a specific layout, called the "IMRaD" format, to communicate empirical research findings. Such articles typically have 4 components:

  • Introduction: sometimes called "literature review" -- what is currently known about the topic -- usually includes a theoretical framework and/or discussion of previous studies
  • Methodology: sometimes called "research design" -- how to recreate the study -- usually describes the population, research process, and analytical tools
  • Results: sometimes called "findings" -- what was learned through the study -- usually appears as statistical data or as substantial quotations from research participants
  • Discussion: sometimes called "conclusion" or "implications" -- why the study is important -- usually describes how the research results influence professional practices or future studies

You should also see an Abstract, or short summary, and a References section with all of the works cited in the article.

Why are keywords important?

By this point in your college career, you have had a chance to search library databases. You understand that you need keywords (not sentences) when you search a database. However, using psychology related keywords might be new territory.

Natural Language vs. Database Language

Natural language refers to the common way that we speak in everyday life. Database language refers to how a database classifies a concept and is usually very technical and academic in nature. Though most databases are great at matching natural language entered with database terminology, it’s important for you to begin recognizing specialized terminology. Some examples include:

 

Natural Language Database Language
Teenager Adolescent
Opiod Addication Opiod Use Disorder
Social WIthdrawal Social Anhedonia
ADHD Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity
Gender Identity Gender Dysphoria

 

Where to Find Synonyms

  1. The Internet: Is your search term or concept called anything else? Look it up in an online encyclopedia to find out. For example, in the Wikipedia entry for "hypertension", the synonym high blood pressure is quickly identified in the opening sentence. This is true for most Wikipedia entries for social science and medical terminology. It is Wikipedia, so exercise caution when using this as a background reading source.
  2. Other background sources: You can also easily find synonyms in other background sources, including your lecture notes, textbooks, and print encyclopedias (yes, they still exist!).
  3. Use database subject headings: If you run a search and find a good article, look at the subject terms listed by the database. Use those terms in subsequent searches. 
  4. Use PsycINFO's Thesaurus: On the Advanced Search page look for the Thesaurus button. When you search for a term or phrase, the thesaurus will give you the subject heading associated with your search. Think of it as giving the language that the database uses to describe your topic. 

Example

  1. Start with your research question:
    Do children of divorce have issues with anger management?
  1. Sort out the major terms. In this case:  
    children AND divorce AND anger management
  1. Make a list of synonyms and related terms for each of your major terms.

    Synonyms and related terms for the word children:

    • child

    • boys

    • girls

  • Synonyms and related terms for anger management might include:

    • anger disorder

    • intermittent explosive disorder

    • anger suppression

    • mismanagement of anger
