guide.name: A Guide to Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Students
guide.description: This guide explores 4 overarching areas: What is AI?, Impacts of AI, Thinking Critically about AI, and a robust offering of other readings/viewings. The intent of the guide is to...

asset.description: Like most of us, you probably have questions about the environmental impacts of generative AI use. Just how much water does that prompt require? How can we put the impacts of data centers in perspective? The answers to these questions, and many more, will continue to shift over time as new technology becomes available. This guide provides current perspectives along with resources to explore. Each section is linked here:

What is a data center? 

Data centers are not new, but new data centers built for AI tasks are rapidly multiplying. According to the Brookings Institute, "Data centers undergird the growing use of AI by storing and processing data, text, images, code, and other information sources." [Current number of data centers plus projected number of centers--global & US]
What is the controversy around data centers?

Most college students are aware that generative AI is harmful to critical thinking skills1 but how, exactly, is it harmful? Current research is starting to paint a pretty solid picture, and it starts with cognitive offloading.

Cognitive offloading2 is the use of an external tool to reduce the mental effort required for a task. Things like using a calculator, using a calendar, using a spell-checker...we use technology to offload mental labor all the time. And it’s not a bad thing. But, what if the mental labor we are offloading is mental labor that we should be developing? Letting AI do our brainstorming, outlining, research, and writing means that we don't get a chance to practice critical thinking skills.

If we adopt AI outputs with minimal scrutiny, we end up in a state of cognitive surrender3 where we let AI override our own judgment. The confident, readymade answers we get from ChatGPT preempt our own intuition and diminishes our willingness to engage in reflective thought. Ultimately, surrendering our own judgments to AI leads us to a state of cognitive atrophy4 where we start losing our capacity for critical thinking, our memory suffers, and our knowledge is replaced by a generic AI-generated view of the world that doesn't reflect our own values and experiences.

 

  1. https://www.edweek.org/technology/students-are-worried-that-ai-will-hurt-their-critical-thinking-skills/2026/03
  2. Barcaui, A. (2025). ChatGPT as a cognitive crutch: Evidence from a randomized controlled trial on knowledge retention. Social Sciences & Humanities Open, 12, 102287). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2025.102287
  3. Shaw, S. D., & Nave, G. (2026). Thinking-Fast, Slow, and Artificial: How AI is Reshaping Human Reasoning and the Rise of Cognitive Surrender. Available at SSRN 6097646. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/yk25n_v1
  4. Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y. T., Situ, J., Liao, X. H., Beresnitzky, A. V., ... & Maes, P. (2025). Your brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing task. arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.08872. https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/your-brain-on-chatgpt/

guide.name: UTC Library Starter Guide
guide.description: An in-depth guide to familiarize patrons with the library’s materials, spaces, services, and resources.

asset.description:
Library Access & Essentials

Finding & Borrowing Materials

Digital Resources, Printing & Scanning

Library Spaces

Services & Service Desks

Having easy access to a library isn’t the same as knowing how to use it. Learning the finer points of using databases instead of search engines takes time, navigating online collections can feel like sinking into digital quicksand, and knowing when to ask library staff for help isn’t always obvious. We get it.

Our starter guide helps build your library confidence, cuts through the guesswork, and familiarizes you with the library’s materials, spaces, services, and resources. By the end, the UTC library will feel like your UTC library.

Using the Guide

There’s no right or wrong way to use this guide. Read through it from beginning to end, or jump to the content that answers your question. Each section stands on its own, so start wherever you’d like.

Getting & Using Your Library Card

A UTC library card is your ticket to checking out everything from books and laptops to camcorders and board games. All for free! 

A MocsID doubles as a library card for current UTC students, faculty, and staff. UTC alumni, retirees, and community members must apply for a library card at the 1st floor Check Out desk.

Check out this page for more information on applying for a library card.

Bonus Tip: Besides checking out materials, students, faculty, and staff can also use their MocsIDs to access the Overnight Study Space, release and pay for print jobs, and access study rooms.

Navigating the Library Homepage

Need to know if the studio’s open or when a library event starts? The UTC library homepage is your home base for staying in the know and finding resources. From our online HQ, you can:

  • Use the Quick Search bar to explore our physical and digital collections
  • Access databases, research guides, course reserves, and more
  • Book a study or meeting room 
  • Chat with library staff
  • Schedule an appointment with a research, writing, or studio specialist
  • Explore upcoming library events

You can also log into your library account from our homepage. 

Using Your Library Account

Save time, avoid late fees, and request materials from other libraries (more on that later) with your UTC library account. After logging into your account via the library homepage with your UTC ID and password, you can:

  • Review currently checked out items 
  • Renew materials 
  • Make interlibrary loan requests
  • Check item due dates

Our Borrow and Return Materials page breaks down loan periods, loan limits, and renewals for specific library borrowers.  

Bonus Tip: At the top of your account page, you can also search our collection, explore journals, and lookup citations.

Searching for Library Materials

Knowing how to search for library materials effectively can mean the difference between finding what you need and wading through pages of irrelevant results. 

While using the UTC Library’s search bar, you can filter results according to format, author, journal title, language, and subject. For example, say you’re looking for Alice Walker’s The Color Purple. You can narrow the results to only see physical, electronic, or audiobook editions. Even better, you can filter searches so that only materials currently on the shelves populate your results. No more finding exactly what you need only to realize it’s already checked out!

Peep this page for more useful info about searching for materials and helpful Quick Search tools.

Finding Books on the Shelves

After a quick search, you see the library has the item you were looking for. Great! Now all that’s left is finding it on the shelves and checking it out. 

Rather than arrange books alphabetically, the UTC Library uses the Library of Congress classification system, which organizes books by subject and groups similar topics together on the shelves. Here’s how it works:

  • Think of the first line of the call number, read alphabetically, as the book’s “country” and “state.” The first letter lets you know which stacks “country” the book is in. The numbers on the first line narrow the book’s location further to a specific “state” on the shelves.
  • The call number’s second line represents its “city.” Beginning with a decimal, this line is organized alphabetically and numerically, with the understanding that the numbers represent decimals rather than whole numbers, so “.A425” is read as “point A four two five.”
  • The last line, the “street address,” is the book’s year of publication. Books with publication dates are ordered chronologically.

So, how do you actually find a book on the shelf?:

  • Search the library catalog for your item and note the call number beneath the title.
  • Using signage posted on either end of library shelves, find the shelf range matching the first letter(s) of the call number.
  • Follow the letters and numbers one by one, from left to right, to find the book.

Need help finding something? Library workers at the 1st floor Check Out desk are more than happy to assist you. Rather than reshelve books yourself, place them on one of the carts on the 1st or ground floors—library staff will thank you!

Accessing Course Reserves

If your instructor has a supplementary class resource at the library, chances are, it’s a course reserve. UTC faculty can place electronic and physical materials on reserve online or in the library behind the Check Out desk.

Here are some must-know guidelines about course reserves:

  • Loan periods for reserve items vary, so check the sticker on the cover or box (or your library account).
  • You can check out up to five reserve items at once.
  • Your MocsID and password are required for off-campus access to online reserves.
  • A viewer like Adobe Reader is required to open PDFs.
  • To find reserve items in the library catalog, use the Quick Search box to search materials by instructor name, course ID (i.e. “ENGL1020”), or keyword.

Even if you can’t remove course reserves from the library, you’re more than welcome to scan or take pictures of materials and check them out again as many times as you need to.

Placing Holds, Requesting PDF Scans, and Making ILL/Purchase Requests

If you ever hear muffled sobbing in the library, it’s either a) finals season or b) someone who discovered the book they wanted is already checked out. We’ve got weighted blankets for the first (seriously, you can/should check out a weighted blanket), and the option to place an item on hold for the second.

When searching for materials in the library catalog, click on your desired title in the search results. Next, along the left side, you’ll see “AVAILABILITY.” Select it, and you’ll have a few options to choose from:

  • Place Hold, to have library staff pull and hold the title for you at the Check Out desk 
  • Make a Request, to make an Interlibrary Loan (ILL) request for items not owned by the UTC Library 
  • Request a PDF Scan, to request a scan of a chapter or entire article

Keep an eye on your inbox; we’ll email you when your items are ready for pickup or download. Also, ensure you’re signed into your library account to see the above availability options.

Not signed in 

Signed in

And while we’re on the topic, here are a some essentials to know about ILLs:

  • If the UTC library doesn’t have a book, video, or audio file you think we should add to our catalog, use the Make a Request form to suggest a purchase. Provide as much information about the item as possible, ensuring you include the correct edition, ISBN, and publication year.

  • You can manage all ILL requests from your library account.
  • Articles and book chapters are delivered electronically as a PDF file. You can review articles for 60 days after receipt and download them up to five times.
  • Print books and DVDs arrive in an average of seven business days, depending on availability from our sharing partners.
  • We hold items for two weeks from the date the item arrives. You’ll receive one reminder email during this period if you haven’t picked up your item.
  • The ILL service cannot serve as a replacement for purchasing textbooks.
  • Renewals are available based on policies set by the lending library. You can request renewals for physical items beginning one week before the due date.

So the next time you don’t see the latest Booktok darling gracing our shelves, just make a request!

Accessing Digital Resources

There’s more to the UTC library than what you see on our shelves. Much more. We also have a variety of online resources, such as databases, guides, ebooks, workshops, and online film/audio collections.

Digital resources you can access from the library homepage include:

  • Databases, searchable collections of ebooks, articles, images, and more. Search for databases by title, keyword, or subject.
  • Research guides, curated starting points for researching specific fields and topics. We’ve also created guides for various UTC courses to help you make sense of assignments and succeed in class.
  • Workshops, online and in-person drop-in tutorials offered in the library throughout the year covering a range of topics, from life organization skills and recording live music to using EndNote and writing annotated bibliographies.

You can access ebooks, audiobooks, and magazines via Libby, giving you the option to check out items without visiting the library (but we love seeing you!). Just download the Libby app, sign into our library using your Mocs ID, and, voila, you’re ready to browse our digital shelves!

For your next movie night, check out our streaming video collection. We’ve got academic videos for research and teaching, classic and modern plays if you’re in the mood for drama, and Kanopy for cinematic classics and arthouse favs.

Bonus Tip: Pump the brakes on endlessly scrolling for your next flick and simplify your search with our Streaming Media Guide, where we’ve compiled UTC-licensed streaming video and music resources and links to freely accessible educational streaming video sites.

         

Printing & Scanning in the Library

No matter where you are in the library, chances are, there’s a printer nearby:

  • Ground Floor: One printer near the DVD collection
  • First Floor: Two printers across from the quick lookup computers, one near the study lounge, and another in the hallway near the Chamberlain entrance
  • Second Floor: Three printers against the columns between the computers and open study space 
  • Third Floor: One printer between the Studio and the Center for Advisement and Student Success

Our printers are all-in-one devices that print, scan, and copy. Send documents to the printer via:

  • MocsPrint Mobile: Upload your file at “mocsprint.utc.edu” from your phone or laptop.
  • Email: Send your document via your UTC email to MocsPrintBW@utc.edu (black & white printing) or MocsPrintColor@utc.edu (color printing).
  • Library Computer: Print directly from any library computer.

To release your print job, just tap your MocsID–or guest printing card—on the small black box at any printer. Black & white prints cost $0.07/page and color prints cost $0.35/page. Remember to load your card with Scrappy Cash via the GET app before printing!

Besides printers, the UTC library has a variety of scanners:

  • Fujitsu ScanSnap V600 Overhead Scanner: Located on the 1st floor near the Chamberlain entrance, ideal for scanning longer documents or books. Scan items to the computer for advanced photo and document editing.
  • Epson Perfection V330 Scanner: Found in the 1st floor Audio Visual room (study room 107), scans to computer for simple document editing and sharing.
  • Epson DS 1630 Document Scanners: Located in the 2nd floor Computer Lab, includes auto feed for quick-scanning multipage documents. Scans to computer for simple document editing and sharing.
  • Epson Expression 11000XL Hi-Res Photo Scanner: Found in the Studio on the 3rd floor, can scan film negatives, slides, and oversized documents. Scans to computer for advanced photo and document editing.

Additional printing and copying services (e.g. fax, binding, postage, etc.) are available at the MOCS Print Center at 400 Palmetto St. near the campus security office.

Study & Meeting Rooms 

Got an upcoming exam to cram for? The library’s got you! Our 1st, 2nd, and 3rd floor study rooms can accommodate individuals and groups of up to 14 people. Meeting rooms and computer labs are also available for larger groups.

Bonus Tip: All rooms include a whiteboard, LCD screen, and HDMI/aux inputs; you can also check out adapters and markers at the Check Out desk.

Use the “Book a Room” link on the library homepage to check room availability and make reservations (as many as two weeks in advance). Once you’ve successfully booked your room, you’ll receive an email confirmation. Reservations are limited to a total of three hours each day.

On the day of your reservation, use your MocsID to access your room. Simply hold your phone or card to the lock for a few seconds and wait for the green light. Physical backup keys are available at the Check Out desk.

Computer Lab 

You won’t find a larger computer lab on campus than the one on the library’s 2nd floor. Not only do we have Windows and Mac desktop computers outfitted with various software, but also a dedicated space for adaptive technology. Resources available in room 206 include text-to-speech (TTS) voices, electronic low-vision aids, speech synthesizers, and screen magnification programs. 

If you need help navigating our computer software, check out our guide for software tutorials, Ebooks, help pages, and downloads. Need a bit more help than the guides provide? Research service desk staff can help with basic software questions. Stop by for a chat or hit us up online. 

Studio 

Lights, camera, ACTION! If you’ve ever wanted to record a podcast, create a documentary, or add green screen effects to creative projects, our Studio on the third floor is your destination station. Studio services include:

  • 3D printing
  • Audio/video/photography suite reservations
  • 1-on-1 consultations
  • Studio workshops

Our self-guided tutorials and tips and tricks help acclimate you to Studio services. For times when you need a bit of help from the pros, Studio tech experts are standing by to assist.  

UTC faculty, staff, and students can also check out high-end studio equipment, including:

  • Cinema camcorder kits
  • Pocket gimbals
  • Camera cages
  • Audio and recording kits
  • Light kits
  • Ring lights
  • Synthesizers

The Studio also provides consultations to staff, students, and faculty. Schedule a tech demo, lecture, or lab session, where Studio staff provide in-person instruction, synchronous classes via Zoom, or develop asynchronous course materials. Book a tech consultation to help get your project off the ground or determine what kind of help you need.

Center for Academic Support and Advisement 

Do you need to take a foreign language course to graduate? Will credits from another institution transfer to UTC? When should you declare a minor? If you’ve got questions, the Center for Academic Support and Advisement has answers. 

Located on the 3rd floor across from the Studio, the CASA is the library HQ for tutoring, supplemental instruction, academic coaching, and student success services and programs. Currently enrolled UTC students can schedule free virtual or in-person tutoring sessions, and CASA accepts walk-ins, too. 

Writing & Communication Center 

Reel in those dangling participles, learn the difference between “you’re” and “your”, and end your idea drought with a brainstorming session. The Writing & Communication Center, found in room 118 of the library, helps UTC students, faculty, and staff polish their papers and ideas at any stage of the writing process.

The WCC offers three writing consultation options:

  • In person: Meet with a consultant one on one.
  • Real-time online consultations: Meet virtually with a WCC consultant. 
  • Written feedback: Upload a draft of your paper, assignment guidelines, and your main concerns for a consultant to review and provide detailed feedback.

You can book all appointments through WCONLINE.

No matter whether it’s a research paper, resume, grant proposal, or presentation, trust us, any writing or communication project can benefit from a writing consultant’s feedback.

Bonus Tip: Access helpful WCC resources and video workshops on overcoming writer’s block, understanding literature reviews, formatting citations, and more.

Special Collections 

Preserving 4,500 linear feet of archival material, over 14,000 publications, and more than 35 terabytes of digitized assets, our Special Collections information specialists help serve the teaching and research needs of the UTC community. Even if you aren’t working on a project, you can trek back through time by exploring our physical and online exhibits. Exhibitions rotate regularly, so there’s always something new to see or look forward to.

Special Collections also manages scholarly communications, open publishing, and affordable course and data management initiatives on campus. In June 2017, the repository accepted joint responsibility for curating the Chattanooga History Collections, which are co-owned by UTC and the Chattanooga Public Library.

Additional services provided by Special Collections include:

  • Ask an Archivist: Ask general questions about collections or services.
  • Schedule Instruction: Faculty can arrange for their classes to visit Special Collections or design an archives-focused instruction session.
  • Request Copies: Submit a request for high-quality digital copies of resources.
  • Exhibition Loans: Request to loan Special Collections materials to display in your museum or library space.

While drop-ins are welcome for several of the library’s services, scheduling an appointment with Special Collections is strongly encouraged. That way, you enjoy priority for limited seating and library staff can pre-pull materials before your visit and help you identify other sources to review.

Check Out Desk 

The Check Out desk is the heart of the library, where you can check out tech, get directions around campus, find materials, access course reserves, and more. Also known as the Circulation Desk, the Check Out desk is on the 1st floor of the library across from the whiteboard drawings (illustrated by our very own staff!).

Materials and services available at the Check Out desk include:

  • Library account management
  • Physical study room key check out
  • Fine payment
  • Laptops & Chromebooks
  • Lost & found
  • Guest computer access

Staff can answer questions about the library or campus via phone, chat, or walk-up.

Research Services Desk 

The next time you need help narrowing your list of library resources, using search keywords, deciding which database to use, or integrating research into assignments, pop up to the Research Services Desk on the 2nd Floor. There, you’ll find librarians with varying academic specialties who teach information skills across the curriculum.

Additional Research Desk services include:

  • One-on-one research appointments for classes
  • Workshops
  • Online tutorials
  • Evidence synthesis consultations
  • Understanding and avoiding plagiarism tutorials

Stop by the desk, shoot us an email, or chat with a research librarian online.

And that’s a wrap on our deep dive into the library’s most popular services, resources, and spaces. If you ever need assistance with anything, no matter how seemingly minor, don’t hesitate to turn to staff for help–we’re always happy to recommend a book, give you the low down on the study spots with the best campus views, or help you find the Douglas St. exit (hint: it’s the doors on the first floor past the security gates to the right of the “University of Chattanooga” stone engraving).

Ableton Live is a digital audio workstation that is geared toward those who want to focus on music production. While Ableton Live is used more frequently for live performances, it also works well as a tool for composing, recording, arranging, mixing, and mastering audio.

Adobe Audition is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who already have audio experience, want more control over their audio than Audacity can provide for vocal/podcast-like editing.

asset.name: Adobe Audition Pathfinder
asset.description: Step-by-step instructions for using Adobe Audition

Audacity is a free, open-source digital audio editor available for Windows, macOS, and Linux. This is an entry-level software that works great for simple audio recording and editing. If you are new to audio editing, we recommend starting with Audacity.

asset.name: Audacity Pathfinder
asset.description: Step-by-step guide for using Audacity,

GarageBand is a digital audio workstation that comes pre-loaded on macOS. While GarageBand has pre-loaded instruments for music production, it is also a great option for voice-overs and podcast recording. GarageBand is a little more advanced than Audacity, as it is used for both audio and music production, but it is a great option for those who have a macOS system and do not want to download additional software.

asset.name: GarageBand Pathfinder
asset.description: Step-by-step guide for using GarageBand

Logic Pro X is a macOS-only software that is available for use in the Studio's Audio Suite. It is similar to GarageBand as it is primarily used for music production, but it provides the user with a larger amount of variety and control over their files. This software is recommended for those who have experience in music production and feel comfortable with multi-track mixing

Adobe Illustrator  is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those interested in creating illustrations, logos, and other vector graphics.

Adobe InDesign is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in print and digital publication design.

Adobe Lightroom Classic is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in quick fixes or batch photo editing.

Adobe Photoshop is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in advanced photo editing or graphic design.

Adobe After Effects is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those interested in creating animations, motion graphics, or visual/special effects for video-based projects.

Adobe Premiere Pro is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in video creation and editing.

Camtasia is video editor, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are beginners to video editing.

Final Cut Pro (MAC ONLY) is an Apple-only software that is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in more advanced video editing than what iMovie offers.

iMovie (MAC ONLY) is an Apple-only software that is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. iMovie is also available pre-installed on Apple computers as the default video editing software.

Please note that the software listed below are outside of the Studio's day-to-day questions we assist with. We will do our best to help, but please be patient and understanding as we may not have the answer you are looking for.

 

3DS Max is a 3D modeling software from the Autodesk software suite. It is primarily used for making 3D animations, models, games, and images.

Adobe XD is part of the Adobe Creative Cloud, which is available to all students, faculty, and staff in the Studio. This software is recommended for those who are interested in user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design for digital applications and websites or are pursuing a career in an industry where Adobe XD is part of the industry-standard software.

AutoCAD is a 2D and 3D computer-aided design (CAD) software from the Autodesk software suite. AutoCad software is typically used in a range of career fields such as architectural design, manufacturing, engineering, and more. 

Fusion is a computer-aided design (CAD) software that is a part of the Autodesk suite that is primarily used for 3D modeling in engineering and manufacturing fields.

Maya is a 3D modeling software that is a part of the Autodesk software suite and is primarily used to create assets for interactive 3d applications, animated films, TV series, and visual effects. 

Revit is part of the Autodesk suite primarily focused on building modeling for architects, landscape architects, structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing engineers, designers, and contractors. 

SketchUp is a 3D modeling computer-aided design (CAD) program that is typically used to design models for architecture, interior design, industrial and product design, landscape architecture, civil and mechanical engineering, theater, film, and video games.

Solidworks is one of the most popular 3D CAD modeling software on the market and used across multiple disciplines for designers and engineers.

Please note that the software listed below are outside of the Studio's day-to-day questions we assist with. We will do our best to help, but please be patient and understanding as we may not have the answer you are looking for.


ArcGIS and ArcMap are cloud-based online geographic information system (GIS) and mapping software that is primarily used to make maps and analyze data from maps.  

Google Earth Pro is the professional version of Google Earth with the ability to import and export GIS data.

Please note that the software listed below are outside of the Studio's day-to-day questions we assist with. We will do our best to help, but please be patient and understanding as we may not have the answer you are looking for.


BlueJ is an integrated development environment (IDE) that is primarily used for educational purposes. It is used to help learn the Java programming language.

Unity is a cross-platform game design engine that supports 2D, 3D, AR, and VR builds.

asset.name: Get help from the Library
Citing Sources

asset.description:
This research guide was put together by UTC Librarians and has links to a variety of resources that you have access to. Use this guide to find:

  • Recommended databases and subscriptions
  • Quick Search box for finding books, articles, movies and more
  • Links to more help

asset.name: JSTOR
asset.description: Scholarly journals in arts, humanities, social sciences, and sciences, excluding full text from the last 3-5 years.

asset.name: Project MUSE
asset.description: Scholarly journals, e-books, and reviews spanning the humanities and social sciences.

asset.name: Women and Social Movements in the United States
asset.description: Primary source documents that chronicle the history of women in social movements in the U.S. between 1600 and 2000.

asset.name: Social Science Premium Collection
asset.description: Social Sciences journal indexes and full text covering subject areas including Politics, Sociology, Education, Linguistics, and Criminal Justice.

asset.name: Google Scholar
asset.description: Search for scholarly literature including peer-reviewed papers, theses, books, abstracts, and articles.

asset.name: Taylor & Francis Journals
asset.description: Scholarly journals in the social sciences, humanities, and sciences.

asset.name: APA PsycINFO w/APA PsycARTICLES
asset.description: Top recommended database for clinical and social psychology. Includes an index of scholarly literature from the American Psychological Association.

asset.name: Sociological Abstracts
asset.description: International literature of sociology and related disciplines in the social and behavioral sciences.

asset.name: SAGE Journals
asset.description: Full text scholarly articles covering social and health science topics including criminal justice, psychology, education, nursing, nutrition, and more.

asset.name: Web of Science
asset.description: Expansive multidisciplinary index to the sciences, social sciences, arts, and humanities. Includes citation analysis and management tools.

asset.name: MLA Directory of Periodicals
asset.description: Information about the journals and book series that publish material related to language and literature.

asset.name: Ethnographic Video Online
asset.description: A comprehensive online resource for the study of human culture, behavior and society around the world. Over 700 hours of streaming video, including ethnographic films, documentaries, select feature films, and previously unpublished fieldwork.
Use for full text options.

Data and Statistics Guide

Find data in library databases and freely available resources by discipline, time periods, and geographies. This guide also provides strategies for searching for data beyond the linked resources.
